marca.titulo: When shoppers can turn the product around, they buy with fewer doubts.
marca.intro: A photo shows one angle; this page shows all of them, in the fabric and finish the shopper picked. The figures below were published by third parties about stores that already use 3D: they are not results of this demo.

resuelve1.p: Velvet changes with the light. The “See the fabric” button brings the camera to the fibre so shoppers see the real sheen before paying, which is where “it wasn't the colour I expected” starts.
resuelve2.p: 6 fabrics × 4 woods × 3 metals: 72 versions of the chair and 112 of the sofa, without a single photo shoot. A new fabric is one more line in the catalogue.
resuelve3.p: The total changes with every choice and the configuration enters the cart as an order line with its price: the same information the warehouse needs.
integra.titulo: It plugs into the product page and cart the brand already has.
integra1.p: The GLB comes from the brand's catalogue (many manufacturers already have one for their renders) or is modelled once per product.
integra2.p: Under 2 MB per product: WebP textures, quantised geometry and a single studio environment. This chair weighs 1.13 MB and the sofa 0.51 MB.
integra3.p: A component that goes where the photo gallery sits today. No plugin, no app: it runs in the phone and desktop browser.
integra4.p: Each option is a SKU variant. When added, the configuration travels as an order line with its price, just like a size or a colour.
integra5.p: The same model opens in augmented reality on Android (glTF) and, with a USDZ copy, on iPhone, to see it in the living room. According to
integra5.p2: , AR made shoppers 65% more likely to buy.
med.fps: Frames per second while turning (screen cap)
med.nota: Measured by me on this page with headless Edge and an integrated GPU, empty cache. On slow 4G (1.6 Mbps) the poster shows at 2.2 s and the 3D at 10.6 s.
proceso.titulo: How I built it and what I measured.
brief.p: A furniture product page where shoppers pick fabric, wood and metal and see the result in 3D under studio light, with the price always in view. Acceptance criteria: velvet has to look like velvet, the first view must weigh under 2.5 MB, it must work with one finger or a keyboard, and it must not drain the battery when nobody touches it.
brief.como: I built it with AI-assisted development: I set the brief, the criteria and the decisions below, and checked every version with full-resolution screenshots and measurements.
dec1.t: I used the model's fibre sheen and added a close-up of the fabric.
dec1.no: I ruled out a fabric swatch photo: it doesn't show how it changes with the light.
dec2.i: A product page is not a scene.
dec2.t: A light studio backdrop, one light with a soft shadow and a slow turn that stops on its own after one revolution.
dec2.no: I ruled out a living-room set and post-processing: they add weight and steal attention from the product.
dec3.i: Phone battery is part of the experience.
dec3.t: On-demand rendering: if nothing changes, no frame is drawn.
dec3.no: I ruled out a continuous 60 fps loop while the image stands still.
pres.caption: First view of the chair: bytes over the network with an empty cache (code served gzip-compressed, as on the host). 27 requests.
pres.nota: The sofa (0.51 MB) only downloads if the shopper picks it. To take the chair model from 1.55 to 1.13 MB, I quantised the geometry and removed an internal label nobody sees.
afuera1: Augmented reality is described, not implemented.
afuera2: The models are public Khronos samples, not a real catalogue; prices and names are examples.
afuera3: The cart is simulated: no payment, stock or shipping.
afuera4: Textures are still WebP; with KTX2 they would use less video memory on modest phones.
afuera5: I tested keyboard, focus and ARIA structure; I did not run tests with users or with real screen readers.
